title: Jeremiah 12:14–17
context: Jeremiah 12:14–17 records a word the LORD speaks “Concerning all my evil neighbors, who touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit”. The neighbors are not named; many readers think of nations such as Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Aram, and 2 Kings 24:2 mentions raiding bands from several of these peoples, though the identification is not certain. The LORD says he will pluck up these nations and pluck up Judah from among them (12:14), then return with compassion and bring each back to its land (12:15). The language of plucking up and building echoes Jeremiah’s commission, “to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (1:10). The promise is conditional: if the nations “diligently learn the ways of my people”, swearing by the LORD’s name as once they taught Judah to swear by Baal, they will be built up in the middle of his people; if they will not hear, that nation will be plucked up and destroyed (12:16–17). Later oracles in Jeremiah also speak of restoring the fortunes of some neighbors, such as Moab, Ammon, and Elam (48:47; 49:6, 39). Readers in both traditions see here a hope that the nations may be joined to God’s people, and questions about the scope of God’s offer to the nations are discussed in the existing boxes at Genesis 12:3 and Isaiah 56:7 rather than reopened. How far the promise was fulfilled in Jeremiah’s era, and how far it looks further ahead, is debated, and these notes do not settle it.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Concerning all my evil neighbors, who touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit: Behold, I will pluck them up from off their land, and will pluck up the house of Judah from among them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks concerning “all my evil neighbors” who touch his people’s inheritance, and says he will pluck them up and pluck up Judah from among them. Arminian readers note that the neighbors are not named, though many think of nations such as Moab, Ammon, and Edom, and they hold the identification loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same uncertainty about the neighbors and observe that God judges both the nations and his own people. They hear the language of plucking up as an echo of Jeremiah’s commission (1:10), named here without harmonizing, and they read the verse as God’s rule over all the nations.

verses.text: It will happen that after I have plucked them up, I will return and have compassion on them. I will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will return and have compassion on them. I will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land.” Arminian readers note that God’s compassion reaches even the nations that troubled Judah, and they see in it God’s sincere desire to restore and not only to judge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same compassion and compare the later promises to restore the fortunes of Moab, Ammon, and Elam (48:47; 49:6, 39). They read the verse as showing that God’s purposes for the nations include mercy after judgment, a hope both traditions share.

verses.text: It will happen, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, ‘As the LORD lives;’ even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they will be built up in the middle of my people.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that if the nations “diligently learn the ways of my people”, swearing by his name as they once taught Judah to swear by Baal, they will be built up among his people. Arminian readers stress the condition and see a real offer to the nations that calls for a genuine response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same condition and read it within God’s purpose to gather the nations to himself, which many of them see fulfilled in the later inclusion of the Gentiles. Both traditions point to the existing boxes at Genesis 12:3 and Isaiah 56:7 for the scope of God’s offer rather than opening a new contrast.

verses.text: But if they will not hear, then I will pluck up that nation, plucking up and destroying it,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “But if they will not hear, then I will pluck up that nation, plucking up and destroying it”. Arminian readers note that the warning shows the response of the nations truly matters, and that refusing to hear leads to judgment, so the promise of the previous verse is not automatic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same warning and read it as a sober reminder that God’s mercy does not cancel his justice toward those who refuse to listen. They observe that both the promise and the warning are framed by God’s word, and both traditions affirm that hearing God is the way of life.
